title: Nzikinziki
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Fish boned, mashed to a paste and cooked into groundnut sauce — a Madi dish especially known in Adjumani, where the fish loses its shape entirely.
longDesc: Nzikinziki is a Madi dish in which the fish is boned, mashed and cooked into groundnut paste, so that nothing recognisable as a fillet survives. It is especially known in Adjumani. This matters beyond the recipe: Madi and Alur are the two West Nile communities for which no dedicated food source exists at all, and this dish is one of the very few Madi preparations documented anywhere. The groundnut sauce follows the universal rule — paste dissolved in cold water first.
ingredients: Cold water, to dissolve the paste
steps: Remove the bones from the fish.
Mash the fish to a paste.
Dissolve the groundnut paste in cold water to a smooth sauce.
Bring the sauce to the boil and cook until ready.
Stir the mashed fish through it, add salt, and simmer to bring the two together.
chefTips: Bone it thoroughly before mashing. Once the fish is a paste you will not find a bone until you bite it.
Mash it properly. This dish is defined by the fish losing its shape — pieces of fish in groundnut sauce is UGA027, a different thing.
Dissolve the groundnut paste in cold water first, as with every Ugandan groundnut sauce.
It is a Madi dish rather than a Lugbara one, and it is especially known in Adjumani.
No quantities are documented. Nothing here is estimated.

Worth stating plainly: Madi and Alur are the two West Nile communities with no dedicated food source anywhere I could find, and this is one of the few Madi dishes that is written down at all. Anything more would need field or oral sourcing, or a Ugandan collaborator.
Smoked or dried fish works as well as fresh and is what a household away from the river would have.
commonMistakes: Leaving the fish in recognisable pieces.
Dissolving the groundnut paste in hot water.
Boiling it hard after the fish is in.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine, which lists nzikinziki among the fish dishes as a Madi dish in which the fish bones are removed, the fish mashed, and it is served with groundnut paste, especially known in Adjumani. That is the entirety of the documented method and no quantities are given.
That article carries only three references, including web archives and blog material, so its detail is treated as a lead rather than as established fact.

No dedicated food source was found for the Madi or the Alur communities in any search. The Wikibooks 'Mujje Tulye from Uganda' project has a Lugbara chapter but nothing for either. That gap is real and is stated rather than papered over.
The dissolve-the-paste-in-cold-water rule is consistent across every Ugandan groundnut source consulted.
reheating: Warm gently with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Fish supplies complete protein, omega-3 and vitamin B12.
Groundnut paste adds plant protein, niacin and vitamin E.
Mashed and boned, so it suits children and anyone who struggles with bones.
culturalNote: West Nile sits where Uganda meets South Sudan and the Congo, and it is the least documented food region in the country. That one Madi dish survives in writing, and only inside an article about a neighbouring people's cuisine, is a fair measure of how much of Uganda's food has never been written down at all.
